title: Boot fit and blister prevention
def: Blisters come from friction, heat, and moisture; boots that fit, dry socks, and treating hot spots early prevent most of them.
look: a warm, rubbing hot spot
heel lifting in the boot
wet socks
use: Break boots in before a trip, wear wool or synthetic socks, stop at the first hot spot, and cover it with tape or moleskin.
not: Do not keep walking on a hot spot, or pop a blister without clean hands and a clean cover.
call: See a clinician for a blister that is red, hot, swollen, or draining pus, especially with diabetes.

title: Sleeping bag temperature ratings
def: A sleeping bag's temperature rating is a lab estimate; most people need a bag rated colder than the night, plus an insulated pad under them.
look: the comfort versus limit rating
a pad's insulation (R-value) for cold ground
damp or compressed insulation
use: Choose a bag rated below the expected low, add a warm pad, wear a dry hat and base layer, and eat before bed.
not: Do not sleep in sweaty clothes or put a down bag in a damp stuff sack for days.

title: Fitting a backpack
def: A pack fits when the hip belt carries most of the weight on the hip bones and the shoulder straps hug without carrying the load.
look: hip belt centered on the hip bones
load lifters snug at an angle
heavy items close to the back
use: Loosen everything, buckle the hip belt first, then snug the shoulder straps, load lifters, and sternum strap. Pack heavy items close to your spine.
not: Do not carry the weight on your shoulders alone or overload for a day trip.

title: Field repair: tape, cord, and needle
def: A small repair kit of tape, cord, a needle and strong thread, safety pins, and a few zip ties fixes most broken straps, torn shells, and gear failures.
look: duct or repair tape wrapped on a bottle or pole
spare cord and a buckle
a needle with heavy thread
use: Patch holes with tape on both sides, sew or pin torn straps, lash broken parts with cord, and keep a wet sleeping bag in a dry bag.
not: Do not ignore a small tear in a shell before rain; tape it now.

title: Rope and cordage basics
def: A length of strong cord lets you hang a tarp, rig a clothesline, lash a splint, or hang food; knowing a few knots makes it useful.
look: about 50 feet of thin, strong cord
rope rated for the job if it holds people
fraying or melted spots
use: Carry cord for camp jobs and learn a bowline, a taut-line hitch, and two half hitches.
not: Do not use utility cord for climbing, rappelling, or holding a person.

title: Binoculars and rangefinders in practice
def: Binoculars help you identify animals and people before acting; a rangefinder measures distance to keep shots within your practiced range.
look: a steady rest when glassing
identifying the whole animal
range checks on landmarks before game appears
use: Glass from a rest, range a few landmarks around your stand, and use binoculars, not a rifle scope, to look at things you are not sure of.
not: Do not use a rifle scope to scan people or unknown movement.

title: Trekking poles
def: Trekking poles take strain off knees on descents, add balance on stream crossings and ice, and can hold up a tarp.
look: elbow at about a right angle on flat ground
longer for downhill, shorter for uphill
tips and baskets for snow
use: Adjust the length to the slope, use the straps correctly, and plant poles ahead on crossings.
not: Do not rely on poles to stop a slide on steep ice; turn back or use proper traction.

title: Saw and hatchet safety
def: A folding saw is safer and more efficient than a hatchet for most camp wood; both need a clear swing zone and a stable work position.
look: a clear arc with no people or branches
wood on a stable base, not held by your foot
sharp tool with a sheath or guard
use: Saw dead, down wood, kneel or stand so a missed swing goes into the ground, and sheath tools when done.
not: Do not chop toward your legs, swing while tired, or cut standing live trees where it is not allowed.
call: Press firmly on a deep cut and get medical care; call 911 for bleeding that will not stop.

title: Winter travel gear
def: Winter trails need traction such as microspikes or snowshoes, insulated boots, extra layers, and more daylight planning.
look: ice under snow on trails
deep snow that makes you posthole
short daylight and fast cooling
use: Carry traction, a warm spare layer, an insulated bottle, and a headlamp, and turn back early.
not: Do not walk on frozen lakes or rivers unless you know the ice is safe and thick.

title: Phone battery and backup power
def: A phone drains fast in cold and when searching for signal; a charged power bank and battery-saving settings keep it working for calls and maps.
look: battery level and temperature
airplane mode when you don't need signal
a power bank and cable in a dry bag
use: Keep the phone warm in an inside pocket, turn on low-power or airplane mode, dim the screen, and carry a charged power bank.
not: Do not let the phone die before you send a location or call for help when you need it.

title: Satellite SOS and messengers
def: Satellite SOS devices and some phones can send an emergency message from places with no cell signal; a personal locator beacon alerts search and rescue directly.
look: a clear view of the sky
the device registered and tested before the trip
battery charged
use: Learn how to send an SOS before you need it, keep it on your body, and use it only for real emergencies.
not: Do not assume a phone has satellite service in your area without checking.
call: Use SOS for life-threatening emergencies; otherwise text or call when you can.

title: Whistle and signal mirror
def: A whistle carries farther than your voice and takes little energy; a signal mirror flashes sunlight to aircraft or searchers miles away.
look: three blasts or three flashes as a distress signal
a whistle on the pack strap or jacket
sunlight for a mirror
use: Blow three blasts and repeat; aim the mirror flash at aircraft or distant searchers using your fingers as a sight.
not: Do not use distress signals as a joke or game near other people.

title: Insect repellent and tick-treated clothing
def: EPA-registered repellents such as DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus on skin, and permethrin on clothing, reduce tick and mosquito bites.
look: the EPA registration on the label
permethrin for clothes and gear, never skin
age limits on the label for children
use: Use repellent on exposed skin as the label directs, treat boots and pants with permethrin, and do a tick check after.
not: Do not put permethrin on skin, spray repellent on a child's hands, or use oil of lemon eucalyptus on children under three.

title: How much water to carry
def: How much water you need depends on heat, effort, and distance; a rough start is about a half liter per hour of moderate hiking, more in heat.
look: dark urine or thirst
hot, dry, or high-altitude conditions
reliable water sources along the route
use: Carry enough to reach the next sure source plus extra, and a filter or tablets to treat more.
not: Do not ration water to the point of dehydration in heat; drink and plan a shorter trip.
